title: [DocDb] Increase in NewOrder latencies in the TPCC runs, after changing ami from centos to almalinux8.8
body:
Jira Link: [DB-9265](https://<redacted-host>/browse/DB-9265)
### Description

After changing YB image ami from centos to almaLinux8.8, the latencies for NewOrder transactions in TPCC runs, have increased by more than 2x. The select latencies have increased from 2.5ms to 10ms.
Comparison report for [TPCC 1k Restore](http://<redacted-host>/report/view/W3sibmFtZSI6ImNlbnRvc19hbWkiLCJ0ZXN0X2lkIjoiMzY5OTIwMiIsImlzQmFzZWxpbmUiOnRydWV9LHsibmFtZSI6ImFsbWFMaW51eDgiLCJ0ZXN0X2lkIjoiMzc3NjQwMiIsImlzQmFzZWxpbmUiOmZhbHNlfV0=) (centos Vs almaLinux8)

@participant3 suggested comparing statement statistics from the two runs.

CentOS 7:
https://gist.githubusercontent.com/participant1/9a0438acdb791052e3b62de0b2caf515/raw/8544528e0d9725ff2cf714dac8b40fa809048de7/centos7_statements.json

Alma 8: https://gist.githubusercontent.com/participant1/7b21883bccdc1e443bfa6b2ecf139fc4/raw/055af9dba74adaf5890a3059dcb27de35a032e35/alma8_statements.json

When comparing these two files using the script below 
```
#!/usr/bin/env python3

import json

from copy import deepcopy

import pprint


def read_json(name):
    with open(name) as f:
        return json.load(f)


def get_statements_map(m):
    assert len(m) == 1
    m = m[0]
    result = {}
    for s in m['statements']:
        s_copy = deepcopy(s)
        q = s['query']
        del s_copy['query']
        if not q.startswith('BACKFILL'):
            result[q] = s_copy
    return result


a = read_json('centos7_statements.json')
b = read_json('alma8_statements.json')

am = get_statements_map(a)
bm = get_statements_map(b)

num_only_in_one = 0
num_common = 0
query_order = []
for k in am.keys() | bm.keys():
    if not k in am or not k in bm:
        num_only_in_one += 1
        continue
    num_common += 1
    a_data = am[k]
    b_data = bm[k]
    query_order.append((k, b_data['mean_time'] / a_data['mean_time']))

query_order.sort(key=lambda t: t[1], reverse=True)

for k, ratio in query_order:
    a_data = am[k]
    b_data = bm[k]

    print(k)
    print("Alma 8 / CentOS 7 latency ratio: %.3f" % ratio)
    print(a_data)
    print(b_data)
    print("\n")

print("Num queries only in one run: %d" % num_only_in_one)
print("Num queries only in both runs: %d" % num_common)
```
I get this output: https://gist.githubusercontent.com/participant1/145f9387494acd79fb20a4982a888015/raw

The statement that is slowed down the most in Alma 8 compared to CentOS 7 (over 14x) is

```
SELECT S_W_ID, S_I_ID, S_QUANTITY, S_DATA, S_YTD, S_REMOTE_CNT, S_DIST_01, S_DIST_02, S_DIST_03, S_DIST_04, S_DIST_05, S_DIST_06, S_DIST_07, S_DIST_08, S_DIST_09, S_DIST_10 FROM STOCK WHERE S_W_ID = $1 AND S_I_ID IN ($2)
```

comments.author: participant1
comments.body:
I also see that the two OSes use different clock sources.

cat /sys/devices/system/clocksource/clocksource0/current_clocksource

shows the following

AlmaLinux 8: `tsc`
CentOS 7: `kvm-clock`

For reference, the kernel versions are:

AlmaLinux 8: 4.18.0-477.15.1.el8_8.x86_64
CentOS 7: 3.10.0-693.5.2.el7.x86_64

The following page has some useful instructions on fine-tuning RHEL 8 for latency-sensitive applications.

https://access.redhat.com/documentation/en-us/red_hat_enterprise_linux_for_real_time/8/html/optimizing_rhel_8_for_real_time_for_low_latency_operation/managing-system-clocks-to-satisfy-application-needs_optimizing-rhel8-for-real-time-for-low-latency-operation

In particular, the clock source discussion is mentioned there.

Another article on changing the clock source: https://repost.aws/knowledge-center/manage-ec2-linux-clock-source

Virtualization type is hvm and instance type is c5d.2xlarge.
According to https://<redacted-host>/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/instance-types.html, c5d instance types use the Nitro hypervisor. And according to https://repost.aws/knowledge-center/manage-ec2-linux-clock-source
> The recommended clock source for the AWS Nitro Hypervisor is kvm-clock.

The following clock_timing program 

```
#include <time.h>
void main()
{
	int rc;
	long i;
	struct timespec ts;

        for(i=0; i<10000000; i++) {
		rc = clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC, &ts);
	}
}
```

produces the following results:

AlmaLinux 8: 
```
$ time ./clock_timing

real	0m0.214s
user	0m0.210s
sys	0m0.002s
```

CentOS 7:

```
$ time ./clock_timing

real	0m0.550s
user	0m0.549s
sys	0m0.001s
```
So the clock is in fact faster to read on AlmaLinux 8 compared to CentOS 7.

comments.body: Some details related to investigating the NewOrder latency increase in 2.20, where we never switched to non-Linuxbrew builds, but where the latencies increased nevertheless with the switch from CentOS 7 to AlmaLinux 8. To evalute the effect of backporting 86ca54435a55dd3373700d6adbf1d5eac4981f0d ( [#20912] DocDB: Use rpc::Strand instead of thread pool token in PeerMessageQueue ), we executed the 1000 warehouse TPCC experiment 7 times and obtained the following latencies: 68.46 75.5 71.56 69.72 69.16 67.46 70.36 The latencies shown in the right-hand side of the graph above (after the regression) are listed here: https://gist.githubusercontent.com/participant1/c7e044d19208ce5608f3163112b25005/raw (captured across different commits). Comparing the latencies with the fix with the baseline using a 2-sided t-test, assuming the variance of the second sample is the same as the first (which is a stricter test in this case compared to assuming the variances are different -- the variance of the post-test sample is really low), we obtained a p-value of 0.02150551563, indicating that this is indeed a statistically significant improvement to the latency (77.64ms to 70.32ms). The t-test was performed using the T.TEST function in Google Spreadsheets with parameters (2, 2) -- 2 tails, the other 2 for assuming equal variances.
